Academic Alerts Analysis

Fall 2025, Harpur College, Binghamton University

Alerts in Harpur

This analysis examines data from all 9,282 Harpur College students and their 35,822 Fall 2025 class enrollments; it focuses on the use and impact of the academic alert system.

An important distinction. The alert system has two very different types of alerts:

  • Medium and High alerts I call “warning alerts”: low exam scores, missed assignments, attendance problems, danger of failing. These are the alerts that matter for intervention, and they are the focus of this analysis throughout.
  • Low alerts are not warnings. These are kudos, no requests for intervention. As shown below, students receiving only low alerts look similar to non-alerted students. Unless otherwise noted, when this analysis refers to “alerts,” it means warning alerts (medium/high).

Who Gets Alerts?

Alerts Track Cumulative GPA

Students who receive warning alerts already have substantially lower GPAs. Low-alert students — those receiving positive feedback — look nearly identical to students with no alerts.

Alert Category Students Mean GPA Median GPA % Below 2.5
No Alert 6,347 3.38 3.48 5.9%
Low Alert Only 1,418 3.61 3.71 1.8%
Medium/High Alert 1,517 2.75 2.84 29.8%

Who Issues Alerts?

Alert system usage is highly concentrated. A small number of departments and instructors generate the majority of alerts.

Departments

Kudos vs. Warnings: Who Issues What?

Most alert-issuing instructors send only warnings, not kudos
Instructor Type N Instructors Percent
Both 75 27.1%
Kudos only 13 4.7%
Warnings only 189 68.2%

Of the 277 instructors who issue any alert, 264 issue warnings while only 88 issue kudos. Kudos account for 45.1% of all alerts (1,851 of 4,103), but they are heavily concentrated:

The top 3 kudos issuers alone account for 27.7% of all kudos. Because kudos are not interventions, they are set aside for the remainder of this analysis. All subsequent analysis focuses on warning (medium/high) alerts.

Instructor Concentration (Warning Alerts)

Among the 264 instructors who issued at least one warning alert, a small group accounts for the bulk of the system’s output. But this concentration tells only part of the story.

Alert Coverage: Instructors vs. Students

Alert system coverage: few instructors, but many students
Metric Count Percent
Instructors who issue alerts 277 / 721 38.4%
Course sections with at least 1 alert 403 / 1835 22.0%
Students in at least 1 alert-issuing class 7,884 / 9,282 84.9%

Only 38.4% of instructors issue alerts, and they teach only 22.0% of course sections. But because alert-issuing instructors tend to teach large classes, 84.9% of all students are enrolled in at least one class where alerts are used. The system’s student-level reach is much broader than its instructor-level adoption suggests.

Alerts and Student Outcomes

The remaining analysis focuses on warning (medium/high) alerts — the alerts meant to flag struggling students and trigger intervention.

The descriptive analysis above suggests alerts correctly identify struggling students in terms of standing and lower gpas. What are student outcomes given alerts or their absence?

Raw Outcomes: Warned Students Do Worse

Grade Distribution

More Alerts, Worse Outcomes

More alerts for a single student should produce greater intervention effort. The grade outcomes for students with multiple alerts are not great, and seem to get worse as the number of alerts grows. Of course, this isn’t because of the alerts - the alerts are symptomatic of how much trouble the student is in. How much intervention is changing outcomes we cannot say, but students with more alerts pass considerably less frequently. Again, this may suggest alerts correctly identify students in need of help, but that help is difficult to provide.

In this plot, pass indicates a grade of D or better; it excludes withdrawals. The pattern is similar if withdrawals are included as failures.

Same Student, Different Classes

The strongest test we can perform with these data is a within-student comparison. About 2,914 students received alerts in some classes but not others. For these students, we can compare outcomes in their alerted vs. non-alerted classes, holding student characteristics constant.

This is not surprising: warning alerts are issued because students are struggling in a particular class. But it means the alert system identifies problems rather than solving them.

What Warning Alerts Miss

Among D/F/W grades where the student had no alert in that class and was never alerted anywhere:

  • 26.4% occur in classes that never issue alerts at all — there is no measurement effort, so struggling students are invisible to the system.
  • 11.9% occur in classes that do alert other students but missed these individuals — a measurement problem where the instructor couldn’t (or didn’t) identify these students as struggling despite flagging others in the same class.

Which Courses Have Unalerted D/F/W Grades?

Some courses have many D/F/W grades with zero alerts issued. Others have strong alert coverage. The pattern varies widely by course and instructor.

Among the 54 courses with 10 or more D/F/W grades, 16 have zero alerts—accounting for 427 D/F/W grades (31.0% of D/F/W grades in high-volume courses). Even in courses that do use alerts, many struggling students go unidentified.

What Actually Predicts Outcomes?

GPA Dominates

Model comparison: GPA only vs. GPA + Warning Alert, by outcome type
Outcome AIC (GPA only) AIC (GPA + Alert) R² (GPA only) R² (GPA + Alert) R² Improvement
D/F/W 12401.9 11838.0 0.272 0.306 12.2%
D/F only 7726.5 7541.0 0.355 0.371 4.4%
W only 7799.2 7483.2 0.055 0.093 70.4%

The D/F outcome (students who completed the course but earned D or F) is distinct from Withdrawal. Students who withdraw are unobserved — we don’t know what grade they would have earned. The models tell a consistent story across all three definitions: GPA dominates, and adding alert status provides minimal improvement.

Predicted Outcomes by GPA and Alert Status

Predicted probabilities by GPA, alert status, and outcome type
GPA No Warning Alert: D/F/W Warning Alert: D/F/W No Warning Alert: D/F Warning Alert: D/F No Warning Alert: W Warning Alert: W
1.5 57% 87% 52% 77% 6% 26%
2.0 32% 70% 24% 50% 4% 20%
2.5 14% 45% 9% 23% 3% 15%
3.0 5% 23% 3% 8% 2% 11%
3.5 2% 9% 1% 2% 2% 8%

At every GPA level, warning-alert students have somewhat higher D/F/W rates. But the gap between GPA levels is far larger than the gap between alerted and non-alerted students at the same GPA. A 3.0-GPA student with a warning alert has better predicted outcomes than a 2.5-GPA student without one.

Summary

Finding Value
Warning-alert students: non-D/F/W rate 60.3%
No-alert students: non-D/F/W rate 94.7%
D/F/W grades from never-alerted students 38.3%
Same student: non-D/F/W rate in non-alerted classes 91.2%
Same student: non-D/F/W rate in alerted classes 80.6%
EOP students receiving warning alerts 40.1%
Non-EOP students receiving warning alerts 15.1%

Summary

  1. Warning alerts identify struggling students, but there is no evidence they improve outcomes. Students with warning alerts fail or withdraw at high rates. More warning alerts per class are associated with worse outcomes, not better probably because the alerts are correctly identifying students in trouble and in need of help.

  2. The same student performs worse in alerted classes than in their other classes. This is expected — alerts follow poor early performance — but it means alerts are reactive, not preventive. Again, it appears alerts correctly identify student problems.

  3. The alert system misses a large share of failing students. 38.3% of all D/F/W grades go to students who were never flagged in any class. Another significant group are in classes with alerts but aren’t identified.

  4. GPA is what actually predicts outcomes. Adding alert status to a GPA-based model provides minimal additional predictive value. Alerts largely reflect information already captured by prior GPA.

  5. Alert usage is concentrated but reach is broad. Only about 38% of instructors issue alerts, but because they tend to teach large classes, 85% of students are enrolled in at least one alert-issuing class.
